items.sentence: The NHS says loperamide slows the passage of food through the gut, which lets the body absorb more water, so stools firm up and become less frequent.
The NHS advises talking to a doctor if loperamide bought over the counter is needed for more than a short time.
items.note: NHS summary: not more than 48 hours without a doctor

items.sentence: The slower movement gives the body more time to take water back from the bowel contents.
Constipation, headache and feeling sick are the commonest side effects, according to the NHS.
Dizziness, tiredness or sleepiness, which alcohol makes more likely
Taking too much loperamide is an emergency: call 999 or go to A&E. If it was taken on purpose, NHS 111 and Samaritans on 116 123 (free, any time) can help.
items.note: NHS: too much can cause serious heart problems; routes are site signposting

items.sentence: MedlinePlus, a US source, says loperamide should not be given to a child younger than 2 years because of the risk of serious breathing and heart problems.
MedlinePlus says people with a prolonged QT interval, a slow or irregular heartbeat or low potassium should tell their doctor before using it.
The NHS says a serious allergic reaction to loperamide is possible but rare.
The NHS advises not driving, cycling or using machinery or tools if loperamide causes dizziness, tiredness or sleepiness.
